title: A God who suffers
hook: the cross says God is not distant from pain

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in the dark. Your line was even darkness can be prayed.

"Jesus wept." In the King James Bible, that's a whole verse, two words long. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, at the village of Bethany. Mary, Lazarus's sister, has just fallen at his feet, crying. So are the people with her. John says Jesus groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and then he weeps. The strange part: In the story, he's about to call Lazarus out of that tomb. He knows how this ends. He weeps anyway.

Christians believe Jesus is God come in the flesh. So when he weeps at Bethany, they see more than a sad friend. They see God crying at a funeral. He doesn't give Mary a lecture on death. He weeps with her. Next, Isaiah, whose suffering servant you met back in year two: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Acquainted with grief: not a visitor to it, a neighbor. Jewish readers read the passage differently, some as speaking of the people of Israel; Christians hear Christ in it. Then the cross. On the cross, Mark says, darkness came over the whole land, and Jesus cried out the opening of another psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Some Christians say this is close to the heart of their answer to suffering, such as it is: not an explanation, but God inside the pain. Theologians put this carefully, and differently. Some say God's own nature cannot suffer, and that Christ suffered in his human nature, truly, as one person. Others speak more boldly of the suffering of God. Churches hold these with care. Both point to one picture: on the cross, God is not watching from far off. Last, Hebrews: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." Christ knows weakness from the inside. Not above the pain, explaining. In it. If grief has you feeling in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

Choose someone you've never met, a name in the news, a stranger in a waiting room, a worn face you passed today, and picture them where they are. If you pray, picture God not above them but beside them, in the chair by the bed, weeping with them the way Jesus wept at Bethany, and say their name to God, nothing else; if you don't, simply picture them not alone.
A God who suffers. The Christian belief that in Jesus, God weeps at a grave and goes to the cross: not distant from pain.
Your line: god in the pain. Not watching from far off, but close. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross in times of suffering, through crucifixes, icons of the crucifixion, Good Friday services and the Stations of the Cross, and some pray with Christ's own cry from Psalm 22.

chat.says: Where is God when someone is suffering? Watching from far away?
options: Christians point to Jesus weeping at a grave and crying out on the cross: God in the pain.
Far away; Christians say God sees our pain only once it's over, never while it's happening.
Nowhere; Christians say God steps in only after a person has stopped hurting.
chat.meaning: Jesus wept at Bethany, and on the cross cried, why hast thou forsaken me. Christians see God not watching from far off, but in the pain.

Bethany.meaning: the village where Lazarus and his sister Mary lived

Lazarus.meaning: Jesus's friend, whom he calls out of the tomb

man of sorrows.meaning: Isaiah's servant, whom Christians read as Christ
